passage:
Hi, I'm Dev, and yes, the turning point was a physics test. I got 18 out of 50, and I had read that chapter three times. I sat there and asked myself, if this isn't working, what could be different?
Then I noticed something. When I read, everything felt easy. When I tried an actual question, I couldn't even start. So reading wasn't teaching me to remember.
That night I read for twenty minutes, closed the book and wrote what I could recall. The gaps were obvious. I did practice questions for the gaps.
Next test I got 34. Mrs Kulkarni asked what had changed, and I said, I stopped rereading and started recalling. She looked surprised, and pleased.

qa.a: Dev felt puzzled and dissatisfied, since reading the chapter three times had not worked.

qa.q: What could Dev try next if recalling from memory stopped helping?
qa.a: Dev could ask Mrs Kulkarni which kinds of questions to practise, because a new signal of no progress would call for another change.

qa.q: How does Mrs Kulkarni see the change in Dev's marks?
qa.a: Mrs Kulkarni looked surprised and pleased when she asked what had changed and heard about the switch to recalling.

grounding: After a low mark a teenager asks what could change, tries practice questions and finds recalling beats rereading.

passage: I'm Noor, and I sit next to Chetan in Class 10. After the half-yearly exams he got 44 in biology, and I saw his face drop. He usually says nothing, but this time he turned to me and asked, "What do you do differently?" I told him I cover my notes and try to write the answers, then check. He looked doubtful. Two weeks later I noticed he'd stopped reading from the book at lunch. Instead he had flashcards, and he'd mutter, flip one, frown, flip back. Sometimes he'd ask me to quiz him. In the unit test he got 67. He didn't say much, just showed me the paper and grinned.

qa.q: What mark did Chetan get in biology at the half-yearly?
What might Chetan have felt when he asked Noor what she did differently?
qa.a: He probably felt disappointed and a bit desperate, ready to swallow some pride and look for another way.

qa.q: What else could Chetan add to the flashcards?
qa.a: Mix in past exam questions and explain answers aloud to a friend, which is more recall practice.

qa.q: How might Noor feel when Chetan shows the paper?
qa.a: Noor likely feels happy and a little proud that the tip helped.

grounding: After a low mark, a student asks what he could change, tries recall practice, and finds it works better than re-reading.

passage:
Monday: Shankar got his physics test back: 39. He had reread the chapter four times. He stayed back and asked his teacher, Gargi Ma'am, "I read so much. What should I change?" She said, "Try closing the book and answering questions. See what you actually remember."

Thursday: At his desk at home, Shankar covered his notes and tried ten questions. He got four right. It was annoying. It also showed him exactly which parts he didn't know. He went back only to those pages.

Two weeks later: The next test came back: 62. Shankar looked at it, then at the stack of practice questions on his desk. Rereading had felt like work. Recalling was actually working.

qa.q: What mark did Shankar get on his first physics test?
How did Shankar feel when he got only four of ten right?
qa.a: He felt annoyed but also more clear, because the mistakes showed exactly what he didn't know.

qa.q: Which choice made the difference, and why?
qa.a: Asking what to change and switching to answering from memory, because it showed his gaps instead of just feeling familiar.

qa.q: How might Gargi Ma'am see the 62?
qa.a: Gargi Ma'am would likely feel pleased and proud that Shankar asked for help and actually tried a new method.

grounding: After a low mark, a student asks what to change, tries practice questions and finds recalling works better than rereading.
